extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, students, and citizens interested in scientific method and the defence/education of science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for what counts as good science, scientific writing, and scientific training — aimed at guiding readers, educators, and citizens in judging scientific works and in cultivating a scientific habit of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific habit of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of forming judgments based on classification of facts, dispassionate investigation, and self-elimination of personal bias — a frame of mind characteristic of the scientific approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquired by careful study of some branch of natural science; even a few hours' weekly study for two or three years can confer insight into method, make one a careful observer, and possibly an original investigator. The aim of education should be to impart appreciation of method rather than mere facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment independent of personal bias
rubrics_metrics.description: A good scientific judgment must be based on clear knowledge of facts and an appreciation of their sequence and relative significance, and should be independent of the idiosyncrasies of the individual mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scientific man must aim at self-elimination in his judgments so that arguments are true for each individual mind. For citizens, forming judgments 'apart from his own feelings and emotions' is an ideal for social welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orderly classification of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Science consists in the classification of facts and the recognition of their relationships and recurring sequences; this method is the unity of all science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any work professing to be scientific should present a classification of facts that leads the reader to acknowledge a logical sequence (a law). The method is applicable across natural, historical, and mental facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions must flow from classification (or be declared assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a conclusion in a scientific work does not flow from the classification of facts, or is not directly stated by the author to be an assumption, it should be regarded as bad science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should either derive conclusions from classified facts or explicitly label them as assumptions. Readers should test works purportedly popularizing science by whether they lead by reason rather than imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular science should teach method, not merely results
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of popular science that merely recites results or appeals to the imagination rather than to reason is 'bad science' or not science at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first aim of any genuine popular scientific work should be to present classifications and systems that appeal to reason before imagination. Recommend applying this test to every popular account of a branch of science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligibility to the logically trained mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Good science will be intelligible to a logically trained mind (given ability to read the scientific language); classics of science often are more intelligible than inferior popularizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers may need patience to learn scientific terminology; comparison of passages can help. Descriptive sciences are generally more accessible to lay readers than exact sciences that require mathematical symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: descriptive vs exact sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive natural sciences (geology, biology) are more easily accessible to the layman than exact sciences (algebra, mechanics), where reasoning is clothed in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing accessibility and the sufficiency of exposition, note whether reasoning depends on mathematical symbols and whether the author provides adequate interpretative aid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method over mere utility — science justifies itself by training of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Science justifies itself not only by practical applications but by training the mind 'to an exact and impartial analysis of facts', which promotes sound citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value scientific work for its educational contribution to method and reasoning, not solely for utilitarian or commercial outcomes. Policy decisions (e.g., funding education) should consider this training value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of scientific method beyond professional scientists
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific method is not peculiar to professional scientists and is applicable to social as well as physical problems; acquiring the scientific frame of mind is essential for good citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizens and non-professionals can and should be trained in scientific method; institutions should provide access to instruction in pure science accompanied by effective teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and unity of science defined by method
rubrics_metrics.description: The field of science is unlimited; its unity consists alone in its method, not in its material: classification and logical treatment of any facts make them scientific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about the domain of science, prefer arguments grounded in methodical classification rather than appeals that certain topics are outside science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward metaphysics without empirical classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphysical systems that lack an accurate classification of facts or are built without empirical foundation are either 'built on air or quicksands' and should be distrusted as scientific accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a metaphysical or philosophical system does not rest on classified, observable facts that lead to convergent judgments, treat its claims cautiously. The multiplicity of competing metaphysical systems is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit ignorance where facts are insufficient; avoid premature system-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Science should frankly admit ignorance in fields where classifications are inadequate; impatience and premature system-making are unscientific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where data and classifications are lacking (e.g., psychology in the author's time), the honest scientific answer is 'I am ignorant.' Resist attempts to 'wall off' difficult fields as beyond scientific method to justify speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method yields practical unanimity; philosophical method risks bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific method, based on classification and observation, tends to lead different individuals to similar judgments; philosophical/internal-cogitation methods are more liable to individual bias and contradictory systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating competing accounts, prefer those grounded in observable classification that allow convergence among investigators; be wary of approaches that rely primarily on internal speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of science often uncovers new phenomena and demands new interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of simple principles often leads to identification of a wider range of previously unnoticed phenomena; every advance opens eyes to new facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of scientific claims should allow for the idea that new classifications can expand the material to be explained; humility and openness to revised interpretation are marks of good scientific attitude.
